concept.name: Geometric mean
concept.definition: The nth root of the product of n positive numbers; the central-tendency measure appropriate when quantities combine multiplicatively rather than additively. In finance, the geometric mean of period growth factors gives the constant per-period growth rate that reproduces the compounded result.
concept.intuition: It is the average growth rate that actually compounds to the observed total. Where the arithmetic mean answers 'average change', the geometric mean answers 'average multiplier'.
concept.mechanics: Multiply the n values and take the nth root; equivalently average their natural logarithms and exponentiate. It is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean, with equality only when all values are identical (AM-GM inequality), so the gap widens with dispersion.
concept.formula: GM = (PRODUCT_{i=1..n} a_i)^(1/n) = exp( (1/n) * SUM ln(a_i) ), for a_i > 0. For returns, apply it to gross returns: g = (PRODUCT (1 + R_t))^(1/n) - 1.
concept.failure_modes: It is defined only for positive values, so it cannot be applied to raw returns that can be negative - one must average gross returns (1 + R) instead. A single zero value makes the whole product zero, and highly volatile return sequences push it far below the arithmetic mean (volatility drag).
concept.misconceptions: The geometric mean of returns is not interchangeable with the arithmetic mean: for +50% and -50% the arithmetic mean is 0% but the geometric mean of 1.5 and 0.5 is about -13.4% per period, which is what the capital actually did. It is also wrong to apply it to negative raw returns directly.
concept.example: An investment with annual returns of +10%, -12%, +90%, -30%, +25% ends at 1.609 times its start; the geometric mean growth factor is 1.0998, i.e., about 9.98% per year, versus a 16.6% arithmetic mean that does not reproduce the final value.
